# Borsuk's Conjecture
Borsuk's conjecture (Borsuk 1932) asserts that every bounded set of n -dimensional Euclidean space of generalized diameter 1 can be partitioned into n+1 pieces of strictly smaller generalized diameter. It is true for n=2 and 3 and for sets with smooth boundary. However, the number of pieces required in the worst case grows at least exponentially in sqrt(n) , so the conjecture is false in sufficiently high dimensions.
For dimension four, Arman *et al.* (2026) proved that every bounded set of diameter 1 in R^4 can be covered by seven balls of a common diameter strictly less than 0.9999. Thus the four-dimensional Borsuk number satisfies 5<=b_4<=7 , while b_4=5 remains open.

Riemann discovered this curvature almost accidentally in his research on heat transfer. In fact, he developed such a curvature tensor for abstract geometries of any dimension n, and Einstein was able to apply Riemann's ideas to his four-dimensional space-time continuum. So we are in the same position as that poor two-dimensional creature. We can make measurements to determine the Riemannian curvature of our universe. Astronomers have been performing such measurements. If we find that the Riemannian curvature is not zero, we know that the geometry is not Euclidean. However, this does not mean that our space is embedded in some higher-dimensional physical space in which it is somehow \"curved.\" When we say, loosely, that \"space is curved,\" we mean only that its geometric properties differ from the properties of Euclidean space in a very specific way given by Riemann's formulas. # BORSUK'S PUZZLE IN 4D: THE ANSWER IS FIVE OR SIX

Borsuk’s question is easy to state. Pick a bounded shape and measure its diameter: the widest gap between any two of its points. Then cut the shape into pieces, each strictly narrower than that diameter. How many pieces will be enough in every case?

In 1933, Borsuk asked whether, in n dimensions, n + 1 pieces always suffice. Fewer cannot work: in an equilateral triangle of side one, every pair of corners sits exactly one diameter apart, so each corner needs a piece of its own. A regular simplex — the n-dimensional version of the triangle — likewise demands n + 1 pieces for its corners. The smallest number that works for every shape goes by the name of Borsuk number, b_n.

## Solved up to three dimensions

Borsuk proved that b₂ = 3: in the plane, three pieces always do. In space, b₃ = 4 was announced by Perkal in 1947 and proved by Eggleston in 1955. In 1993, though, Kahn and Kalai proved the guess wrong in high enough dimensions.

That leaves an awkward gap. Dimension four is now the smallest case still unanswered.

## A bound that keeps falling

For four dimensions, the answer is at least five (the corners of the four-dimensional simplex). The question is how many pieces are enough. Lassak’s 1982 bound, b_n ≤ 2^(n−1) + 1, gave nine. Tolmachev and Voronov cut it to eight in May 2026. In October 2026, Arman, Bondarenko, Prymak and Radchenko covered every four-dimensional shape of diameter one with seven balls, each of diameter less than 0.9999: seven.

Logan Chalmers, at the University of Otago in New Zealand, now proves that six pieces always suffice. So the four-dimensional Borsuk number is five or six.

# Borsuk's Conjecture
Borsuk's conjecture (Borsuk 1932) asserts that every bounded set of n -dimensional Euclidean space of generalized diameter 1 can be partitioned into n+1 pieces of strictly smaller generalized diameter. It is true for n=2 and 3 and for sets with smooth boundary. However, the number of pieces required in the worst case grows at least exponentially in sqrt(n) , so the conjecture is false in sufficiently high dimensions.

The Borsuk number b_d is the least integer m such that every bounded set of generalized diameter 1 in R^d can be partitioned into m subsets of strictly smaller generalized diameter. The vertices of a regular simplex show that b_d>=d+1 . Borsuk's conjecture is the assertion b_d=d+1 .

Abstract. We prove that every bounded set of diameter one in four-dimensional Euclidean space can be covered by seven balls of diameter strictly smaller than 0.9999. ###### Abstract.

Can every set of diameter one in four dimensions be split into at most five parts of smaller diameter? Three parts suffice in the plane and four in three-dimensional space. In four dimensions five parts are sometimes necessary. We prove that six always suffice, improving the previous upper bound of seven. For small circumradius we use six cones. For large circumradius five balls meet every diametral pair of a compact set. At intermediate radii we bound the diameter of each part by the diameter of a rational polytope. The theorem is formalised in Lean.

###### Key words and phrases:

Borsuk’s problem, diameter, circumradius, geometric partitions

###### 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification

Primary 52C17; Secondary 52A20

## 1. Introduction

Can every set of diameter one in \mathbb{R}^{n} be split into at most n+1 parts of smaller diameter? Borsuk [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.17375v1#bib.bib3)] asked this question in 1933. The vertices of a unit equilateral triangle need three parts, since any two are a unit apart. For the same reason, the vertices of a regular n-simplex need n+1 parts.

Write b_{n} for the least number of parts that always suffices. Borsuk proved b_{2}=3. Notes

Borsuk asked in 1933 whether every bounded set of positive diameter in R d can be partitioned into d \+ 1 pieces, each of strictly smaller diameter [[Borsuk1933]]() . Writing b ( d ) for the least number of pieces that always suffices, the question here is the first unresolved instance of that problem: is b ( 4 ) = 5 ?

seltz.snippet:
The diameter of a shape is its greatest width: the largest distance between two of its points. A disc of radius one has diameter 2. Cut the disc into pieces, and the question is how many pieces it takes before every piece is strictly narrower than the whole.

Two are not enough. Cut along a diameter and each half still contains that diameter. Cut in any other way, with any wiggling boundary, and the answer is the same: one of the two pieces contains two opposite points of the rim, so it is still 2 wide. Three are enough. Three sectors of 120° each have a greatest width equal to the chord across the sector, 3\sqrt3, about 0.866 of the diameter.

Fig. 1 A disc of radius one cut into two halves, each still holding a full diameter, and into three sectors of 120°, each narrower than the disc.

Karol Borsuk asked in 1933 whether that pattern holds in general: can every bounded set in dd dimensions be split into d+1d + 1 pieces, each of smaller diameter than the set? ultimate.snippet:
The paper proves improved upper bounds for Borsuk numbers, including b(4) ≤ 6, b(5) ≤ 12, and an analytic improvement over Lassak’s bound in every dimension n ≥ 4.

For dimensions four and five, the author uses three points at which a set touches its smallest enclosing ball. A geometric argument shows that, after an isometry, the set lies within a family of bodies described by four parameters. The parameter range is divided into finitely many boxes, and each box is assigned a rigorous outer approximation of the corresponding bodies. Power diagrams partition these approximations into six pieces in dimension four and twelve in dimension five. Computer-assisted verification—using rational arithmetic and carefully controlled interval and floating-point calculations—certifies that every piece has diameter strictly less than one. Abstract
Can every set of diameter one in four dimensions be split into at most five parts of smaller diameter? Three parts suffice in the plane and four in three-dimensional space. In four dimensions five parts are sometimes necessary. We prove that six always suffice, improving the previous upper bound of seven. For small circumradius we use six cones.
